No.52

Is "Living in the Present" Just a Comforting Phrase?

The past can be learned from and the future prepared for; bring the step you can take back into this moment.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

I asked Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva:
Is "living in the present" just a phrase to comfort people?

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

"You ask:
'Is living in the present
only a phrase of comfort?'
I say:
if it only hangs on the lips,
it is indeed just a phrase;
if it can be practiced in the heart,
it is a discipline.

Among the sufferings of beings,
some are suffered today;
yet many sufferings
come from yesterday, already gone,
and tomorrow, not yet come.
Insulted yesterday,
today one relives the insult again and again;
tomorrow has not arrived,
yet today one already fears it.

A thing happens only once,
but the heart makes it
happen a hundred times.
So what is called the present
does not tell you
to forget the past,
nor tell you
not to think of the future.

Rather:
the past is for understanding,
not for living in;
the future is for preparing,
not for suffering in advance.
Some say:
'If we live in the present,
why plan for tomorrow?'
This is not the present.

Saving money today
is today's deed;
studying today
is today's deed;
treating an illness today
is today's deed;
preparing today for tomorrow
is still acting in the present.

What truly takes people out of the present
is not planning the future,
but a heart that has already run off
into things that have not happened,
fearing them over and over.
Others say:
'If we live in the present,
do not think about the past.'
Nor is this so.

If there were faults in the past,
reflect on them;
if there were wounds in the past,
heal them;
if there was kindness in the past,
remember it with gratitude.
But do not let yesterday
replay every day,
until today too
becomes yesterday's prisoner.

Remembering
and being trapped
are not the same thing.
If you were once hurt by someone,
living in the present
is not telling yourself:
'It's nothing,
it's all over.'
It is knowing:
'It truly happened,
and I was truly hurt.

But the me of today
can decide
how to take the next step.'
This
is not escape,
but taking back this moment.
If you worry about the future,
neither is it telling yourself:
'Don't think about anything;
things will work themselves out.'
Rather, ask:
'Right now, what is there
that I can do?'
What can be done,
do;
what cannot be done,
set aside for now.

Wisdom is not
having no worries;
it is knowing
what can be dealt with now,
and what can only wait for now.
Beings often think:
when I have money,
I will be at peace;
when I have a family,
I will be at peace;
when this is settled,
I will be at peace;
when all my problems are solved,
then I will truly live.

Yet as soon as one thing ends,
another arises.
If you must wait
until life has no problems
before allowing yourself to rest,
then in a whole lifetime,
what day will you ever live?
So practicing the present
is not because
the future does not matter;
it is precisely because life is impermanent
that today matters.

When you eat,
know that you are eating;
when you are with others,
know that you are together now;
when the heart is sad,
know that you are sad;
when the heart is glad,
know that you are glad.

Not every moment
needs to be happy;
only let every moment
not deceive your own heart.
The present is not happiness;
the present is truth.
If there is suffering today,
deal with today's suffering;
if there is joy today,
know that this joy too is impermanent.

Not chasing,
not refusing,
knowing it comes,
and knowing it goes —
this is cultivating the heart.
Therefore I say:
living in the present
is not comforting you that
'everything will get better';
it is reminding you:
whether the future is good or bad,
the only place you can truly set your hand
is always now.

Yesterday cannot be changed,
tomorrow has not come;
but a thought this moment,
a word this moment,
a deed this moment
is becoming
the cause of the next.
So the principle of cause and effect
too does not leave the present.

If you ask:
'Life holds so much suffering —
how can I live in the present?'
You need not demand of yourself
that you always stay settled.
When the mind runs off,
know that it has run off,
and come back.

When it runs off again,
know it again,
and come back again.
It is not never being scattered,
but each time you are scattered,
still knowing to return.
That is all.
Do not take this lightly.

A lifetime
seems to be decades;
what is truly lived
has only ever been
one present moment after another.
Therefore:
the past can be learned from,
not dwelt in;
the future can be prepared for,
not clung to;
the present can be acted in,
not lost.

This is not a phrase of comfort.
It is the only place
where beings can truly
set their hearts, choose,
and change."

🔶Plain Rendering

You ask: "Is living in the present just a phrase to comfort people?" I say: if it only stays on the lips, it really is just a phrase; but if it can be put into practice in the heart, it becomes a real discipline. Some of beings' suffering is happening right now; but much of it comes from yesterday, which has already passed, and from tomorrow, which has not yet arrived.

You were insulted yesterday, and today you keep enduring that insult again and again; tomorrow has not come, and today you are already afraid of it. Something happened only once, but the mind makes it happen a hundred times. So living in the present does not mean forgetting the past, nor not thinking about the future. It means: the past is for understanding, not for living in; the future is for preparing, not for suffering in advance. Some people say: "If we live in the present, why plan for tomorrow?"

That is not the present. Saving money today is today's action; studying today is today's action; getting treatment today is today's action; preparing today for tomorrow is still acting in the present. What truly takes people out of the present is not planning for the future, but the mind running off into things that have not happened yet and fearing them again and again. Others say: "If we live in the present, we shouldn't think about the past."

That is not right either.
If there were mistakes in the past, reflect on them;
if there were wounds, heal them;
if there was kindness, be grateful for it.
But do not let yesterday replay every day,
until today also becomes yesterday's prisoner.
Remembering and being trapped are two different things.
If you were once hurt by someone,
living in the present is not telling yourself:
"It's fine, it's all over."

It is knowing:
"It really happened, and I really was hurt.
But the me of today can decide how to take the next step."
This is not running away, but taking back this moment.
If you are worried about the future,
it is also not telling yourself:
"Don't think about it; it will all work out somehow."
Instead, ask:
"Right now, what can I do?"

What you can do, do;
what you cannot do, set aside for now.
Wisdom is not having no worries;
it is knowing what can be handled now and what can only wait for now.
People often think:
once I have money, I'll be at ease;
once I have a family, I'll be at ease;
once this is settled, I'll be at ease;
once all my problems are solved, then I'll really live.

But as soon as one thing is finished, another comes along. If you must wait until life has no problems before you let yourself be at peace, then over a whole lifetime, when will you ever really live? So practicing the present is not because the future is unimportant; it is precisely because life is impermanent that today matters. When you eat, know that you are eating; when you are with others, know that you are together right now; when you are sad, know that you are sad; when you are happy, know that you are happy.

Not every moment has to be happy; you only need to not deceive your own heart in each moment. The present is not happiness; the present is what is real. If there is suffering today, deal with today's suffering; if there is joy today, know that this joy is impermanent too. Not chasing, not resisting; knowing when it comes, and knowing when it goes. This is cultivating the heart. So I say: living in the present is not comforting you that "everything will be fine"; it is reminding you: whether the future turns out well or badly, the only place you can truly start is always now.

Yesterday cannot be changed, tomorrow has not come; but a thought in this moment, a word in this moment, an action in this moment is becoming the cause of the next moment. So the principle of cause and effect is not separate from the present either. If you ask: "Life has so much suffering — how can I live in the present?" You do not need to demand that you always stay settled. When the mind wanders off, notice that it has wandered, and bring it back.

When it wanders off again, notice again, and bring it back again. It is not about never being distracted, but about always knowing to come back each time you are. That is all it is. Do not underestimate this. A lifetime looks like several decades; but what is truly lived has only ever been one present moment after another. Therefore: the past can be learned from, but not stayed in; the future can be prepared for, but not clung to; the present can be acted in, but must not be missed.

These are not words of comfort. This is the only place where beings can truly set their intention, choose, and change.
